enzyme-structure-s1.title: Swapping one amino acid in enzyme E
enzyme-structure-s1.html:
Enzyme E breaks down substrate S. The end of S that enters the active site carries a negative charge. Substrate T has the same shape and size as S, but that end is uncharged. In the original enzyme, position 102 is lysine, whose side chain is positively charged and lines the active site. Position 100 is glycine, which has the smallest side chain (a single hydrogen atom) and also lines the active site. Position 245 is on the outer surface, far from the active site.

Researchers made five versions of E, each with one amino acid swapped, and measured product formed at 30 °C and pH 7 with the same amount of enzyme and substrate in every trial. Values are means of 4 trials.

items.q: Which statement best describes the data for variants 1, 2 and 3 with substrate S?
options: A positive-for-positive swap changed little, but losing or reversing the charge at 102 cut output with S by over 90%.
Any change at position 102 cut product formation with S by more than 90%, whatever side chain replaced lysine.
Replacing lysine 102 lowered product formation with S and with T by about the same proportion in each of the three variants.
Product formation with S fell in proportion to how much larger the new side chain was than lysine's side chain.

items.q: With substrate S, variant 3 forms product at what percentage of the original enzyme's value? Round to one decimal place.
Variant 2 makes almost no product from S but makes product from T at nearly the original level. Which reasoning best explains this?
options: The negative side chain at 102 repels the negative end of S; T's uncharged end did not rely on an attraction at 102.
Glutamate's side chain is larger than lysine's, so it blocks S from entering the active site but leaves room for the slightly smaller T.
Swapping position 102 unfolded the whole enzyme, and T is able to bind to an unfolded protein while S is not.
T is the enzyme's true substrate, so a change in the active site affects S, which is acted on by accident.

items.q: Which conclusion about variant 5 is best supported by the data?
options: The large side chain at 100 reshapes the pocket, so neither substrate fits well, whatever its charge.
The tryptophan side chain adds a negative charge that repels both substrates, as glutamate did in variant 2.
Position 100 lies far from the active site, so the drop is more likely to come from a change in the amount of enzyme added to each trial.
Tryptophan makes the enzyme hold substrate more tightly, so the products stay bound and are not released.

items.q: What does variant 4 contribute to the study?
options: It shows a swap far from the active site barely changed output, tying the large drops in other variants to the active site.
It shows that serine is required for the enzyme to fold, since output with S fell by more than half when serine was removed.
It serves as the negative control for the whole study, because it contains no working enzyme and measures the product formed without catalysis.
It shows that the enzyme's output depends on the substrate's charge, since S and T gave very different results in this variant.

items.q: Which model of substrate binding do the data best support?
options: Induced fit: the lobes close around the substrate when it binds, so the enzyme's shape changes during binding.
Lock and key: the active site has a fixed shape, and the substrate fits it without the enzyme moving.
The substrate changes shape to fit the enzyme, while the enzyme's lobes stay where they were.
The enzyme changes shape in the same way whenever any molecule that is small enough to enter the cleft is present.

items.q: Molecule L is the same size as G but lacks one –OH group. The gap barely closes and no product forms. Which explanation is most consistent with these data?
options: Without that –OH, a hydrogen bond to an active-site side chain is lost, so binding does not trigger the full shape change.
Molecule L is too large to enter the cleft, so it stays outside and the lobes remain open.
Molecule L binds the active site more tightly than sugar G does, and this tight binding locks the two lobes in their open position.
Molecule L has a positive charge that repels the lobes and pushes them farther apart.

items.q: A variant of enzyme H has its lobes stuck at a 0.9 nm gap before any substrate is added. What is the most likely effect on product formation, and why?
options: It falls, because sugar G can no longer get into the closed cleft to reach the active site.
It rises, because the enzyme is already in the shape it takes when the substrate is bound.
It stays the same, because the gap matters after the product has been released, not during binding.
It rises, because water molecules can no longer enter the cleft and compete with G for space there.

items.q: A student claims the active site of enzyme H is a rigid mold that fits G exactly. Which observation in the table most directly contradicts the claim?
options: The gap between the lobes shrinks from 2.6 nm to 0.9 nm when G is added.
Molecule M, about twice the size of G, makes no product.
Water is present in each of the samples but is not joined to anything.
Each gap in the table is the mean of six measurements rather than one.

items.q: Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
options: It breaks lactose but not maltose or sucrose, though each of the three is a disaccharide containing glucose.
The enzyme breaks any disaccharide that contains glucose, but it works fastest on lactose.
The enzyme breaks maltose and sucrose at the same rate, and lactose at a slightly higher rate.
The enzyme still breaks lactose after it has been boiled, but at a lower rate than when it has not been boiled first.

items.q: Using tube 5 to correct for glucose that is present without the enzyme, what concentration of lactose (in mM) was broken down in tube 1 in 10 minutes? Give one decimal place.
Why did the researchers include tube 4?
options: To show the folded enzyme is needed, so tube 1's glucose comes from the enzyme, not a heat-stable substance.
To show that lactose breaks down on its own when it is heated, so that heat alone could explain the glucose found in tube 1.
To measure how much glucose the enzyme sample contained before it was added to any of the sugars.
To show that the enzyme works faster at high temperature, since boiling speeds up the movement of molecules.

items.q: Lactose and maltose are both disaccharides of almost the same size, and both contain glucose. Which reasoning best explains why the enzyme breaks only lactose?
options: Galactose and glucose differ in how their –OH groups point, and the active site's side chains match lactose's pattern.
Maltose is too large to enter the active site, because two glucose units take up more space than galactose and glucose.
Maltose has a positive charge and lactose a negative charge, and the active site is lined with positive side chains.
The enzyme is used up after breaking the first disaccharide it meets, and in each tube lactose happened to reach the active site first.

items.q: Which description fits an enzyme acting as a catalyst?
options: It speeds up a reaction and comes out of the reaction with its structure unchanged.
It supplies the atoms that become part of the products of the reaction it speeds up.
It speeds up a reaction by being broken down into smaller pieces as the reaction runs.
It changes which products a reaction makes, so the reaction yields different molecules.

items.q: An enzyme's active site is lined by a positively charged side chain at its base and a patch of nonpolar side chains along one wall. Which molecule is most likely to be its substrate?
options: A molecule with a negatively charged group at one end and a nonpolar ring along one side
A molecule with a positively charged group at one end and a nonpolar ring along one side
A molecule with a negatively charged group at one end and several polar –OH groups along one side
A molecule with no charged groups and several polar –OH groups spread over its surface

items.q: In an enzyme, amino acid 310 is far from the active site, but its side chain forms an ionic attraction that holds two folded parts of the protein together. Amino acid 310 is replaced with one that has no charge. What is the most likely result?
options: Folding near the active site may shift, changing its shape and lowering how well the substrate binds.
Nothing changes, because amino acids that do not line the active site have no effect on whether the substrate binds.
The enzyme becomes able to bind many more kinds of substrate, because the active site is no longer held in place.
The substrate binds amino acid 310 instead of the active site, because the charge that blocked it is gone.

items.q: A human enzyme is kept at 70 °C for 10 minutes and then cooled to 37 °C. Its substrate is added, and almost no product forms. Which explanation is best?
options: Heat broke weak bonds holding the protein's fold, and the active site did not regain its shape on cooling.
The heat broke the peptide bonds of the enzyme, leaving free amino acids that are unable to bind the substrate.
At 37 °C the molecules move too slowly for the substrate to reach an enzyme that was heated.
The heat used up the enzyme's stored energy, so it has no energy left to change the substrate into product.

items.q: Two different enzymes in the same cell both bind glucose, but each makes a different product from it. Which explanation is most consistent with how enzymes work?
options: Each active site holds glucose in a different orientation, placing different bonds near its reactive side chains.
Glucose changes its own shape before it binds, so each enzyme receives a different form of the same sugar.
One of the two enzymes is a catalyst and the other is not, so just one of them changes glucose into a product.
The two enzymes have identical active sites, but they sit in different parts of the cell, which decides the product.

items.q: Select the two statements that correctly describe an enzyme-substrate complex.
options: The substrate is held in the active site by weak attractions such as hydrogen bonds and ionic attractions.
The active site may change shape slightly to grip the substrate more closely.
The substrate is joined to the enzyme by covalent bonds that become part of the product.
The complex lasts as long as the enzyme exists, so each enzyme acts on one substrate molecule.
The complex forms when any molecule of about the right size enters the active site.

items.q: Some RNA molecules speed up reactions much as protein enzymes do. Which feature must such an RNA catalyst share with a protein enzyme?
options: A folded 3-D shape with a binding pocket whose shape and chemistry match its substrate
A chain of amino acids whose side chains line a pocket where the substrate binds
Peptide bonds that join it to the substrate for as long as the reaction runs
A set of positively charged side chains that attract any negatively charged molecule nearby

items.q: An enzyme from a deep-sea fish and the matching enzyme from a mouse catalyze the same reaction. The two proteins differ at 40 of their 330 amino acids, but none of the differences are in the active site. Which claim is most reasonable?
options: Their active sites are probably very similar, while the other differences may change how stable the fold is.
The two enzymes are unlikely to catalyze the same reaction, because a protein's job depends on its whole sequence.
The fish enzyme probably binds a different substrate, since 40 changes are enough to change any active site.
The differences outside the active site have no effect on the enzyme, because those amino acids do not touch the substrate.

items.q: A drug molecule has nearly the same shape and charge pattern as an enzyme's substrate, so it binds the active site, but the enzyme cannot change it into product. The drug is added to a tube of enzyme and substrate. Predict the change in each variable.

variables.name: Number of active sites holding the substrate at any moment
Product formed per minute
Total number of enzyme molecules in the tube

items.q: What is the rate of oxygen production with fresh liver extract during the first 30 seconds, in mL per second? Give two decimal places.
With fresh liver extract, oxygen production slows after 90 seconds and nearly stops by 180 seconds. Which explanation is best supported by the data?
options: Nearly all the hydrogen peroxide has been broken down, since the total is close to the 27 mL possible.
The catalase has been used up by the reaction, since each enzyme molecule can break down one hydrogen peroxide.
The oxygen produced has denatured the catalase, since the rate falls as more oxygen builds up in the flask.
The liver extract has run out of energy to give the reactants, since the rate drops steadily over time.

items.q: What is the main purpose of the flask with water instead of a catalyst?
options: It shows how much oxygen forms with no catalyst, the baseline the other flasks are compared with.
It shows that hydrogen peroxide breaks down quickly on its own, so a catalyst is not needed.
It replaces the boiled extract, so the experiment needs just one flask without a working catalyst.
It measures how much oxygen dissolves in water, which is then added to the other flasks' totals.

items.q: Which claim is best supported by comparing the manganese dioxide flask with the other flasks?
options: It speeds the reaction compared with water, though with these amounts more slowly at first than fresh extract.
Manganese dioxide is not a catalyst, because it is not a protein and has no active site to bind hydrogen peroxide.
Manganese dioxide and boiled extract work the same way, because both raised oxygen output above the water flask.
Manganese dioxide releases more energy from each hydrogen peroxide molecule than catalase does, so its rate keeps on rising longer.

items.q: At 180 seconds the student adds another 5 mL of 1.5% hydrogen peroxide to the fresh-extract flask. What is the most likely result?
options: Oxygen production speeds up again, well above its rate just before, because the catalase was not used up.
Oxygen production stays near zero, because the catalase was used up breaking the first 5 mL.
Oxygen production speeds up but stops after 0.2 mL, because each catalase molecule can act a few more times.
Oxygen production slows further, because adding more reactant dilutes the catalase in the flask.

items.q: What is the activation energy of the reaction without the enzyme, in kJ/mol?
By what percentage does the enzyme lower the activation energy? Give a whole number.
Based on the graph, how does the enzyme change the reaction?
options: It lowers the peak but leaves the reactant and product levels alone, so 25 kJ/mol is released either way.
It lowers the energy of the products, so the reaction releases more energy when the enzyme is present.
It raises the energy of the reactants so they start closer to the peak and need less energy to react.
It lowers both the energy peak and the product level by the same amount, so the energy released by the reaction is unchanged.

items.q: The same reaction can also run backward, from products to reactants. Using the graph, how does the enzyme affect the backward reaction?
options: It lowers its activation energy from 100 to 55 kJ/mol, so the enzyme speeds the backward reaction too.
It has no effect on it, because an enzyme's active site binds just the reactants of the forward reaction and not the products.
It lowers its activation energy from 75 to 30 kJ/mol, the same values as for the forward reaction.
It raises its activation energy, which is why the enzyme makes the reaction run in the forward direction.

items.q: What does the highest point on each curve represent?
options: The transition state, the least stable arrangement on the path
The moment the products are released from the enzyme's active site
The energy the enzyme adds to the reactants to start the reaction
The total energy stored in the products once the reaction is finished

items.q: Which statement best describes the data?
options: Output stayed between 4.6 and 4.8 mmol per batch, with no steady decline.
Glucose output fell by about half between the first batch and the sixth batch.
Output rose with each batch as the enzyme got better at binding sucrose.
Glucose output was highest in the last batch and lowest in the first batch.

items.q: Which conclusion do the data most directly support?
options: Invertase is not used up: the same enzyme molecules kept making glucose batch after batch.
Invertase lowers the activation energy of sucrose breakdown by about 4.8 kJ/mol in each batch.
Invertase becomes part of the glucose it makes, so the beads lose some enzyme with each batch.
Invertase acts on sucrose but not on other sugars, since glucose came out of each of the six batches.

items.q: How much glucose, in mmol, did the column produce over all six batches? Give one decimal place.
About how many glucose molecules did each invertase molecule produce over the six batches? (28.4 mmol = 2.84 × 10⁻² mol.)
options: About 4 million (4 × 10⁶)
About 4 thousand (4 × 10³)
About 1
About 4 billion (4 × 10⁹)

items.q: What is activation energy?
options: The energy reactants need to reach the transition state before becoming products
The energy a reaction releases as its reactants are turned into products
The energy that an enzyme adds to its substrate so that the substrate is able to react
The energy stored in the bonds of the products once the reaction is complete

items.q: Breaking sucrose into glucose and fructose releases energy, yet a bowl of table sugar stays sucrose for years. Which explanation is best?
options: Its activation energy is high, so at room temperature almost no sucrose reaches the transition state.
The reaction absorbs energy overall, so it happens just when energy is supplied from outside.
Sucrose is a product of this reaction, not a reactant, so the reaction is unable to start.
The glucose and fructose re-form sucrose as fast as it breaks, so the amount of sucrose looks constant.

items.q: Both heating a reaction and adding an enzyme make it go faster. How do the two differ?
options: Heating gives more molecules enough energy to clear the same barrier; an enzyme lowers the barrier.
Heating lowers the activation energy, while an enzyme gives the substrate the extra energy it needs to react.
Heating changes which products the reaction makes, while an enzyme keeps the products the same.
Heating works for reactions that release energy overall, while an enzyme works for reactions that absorb it.

items.q: A student measures the product of an enzyme reaction every minute: 0, 12, 22, 29, 33 and 35 µmol at 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 minutes. Which statement best describes the reaction rate?
options: It is highest in the first minute (12 µmol/min) and falls as substrate is used up.
It is constant at 7 µmol/min, the total product divided by the total time.
It rises each minute, because the amount of product goes up each minute.
It is highest in the last minute, when the most product is present in the tube.

items.q: Select the three ways an active site can lower the activation energy of a reaction.
options: Holding two reactants close together in the orientation in which they react
Bending or straining bonds of the substrate toward the shape of the transition state
Placing charged or polar side chains next to the bonds that change
Transferring heat from the enzyme to the substrate so it moves faster
Lowering the energy of the products so more energy is released
Adding energy from the enzyme's own bonds, which break as the reaction runs

items.q: An enzyme is added to a tube in which a slow reaction that releases energy is running at 25 °C. Predict the change in each variable.

variables.name: Activation energy of the reaction
Energy released per mole of reactant that reacts
Time needed to make 1 mmol of product
Amount of enzyme in the tube after 1 hour

items.q: A student claims that enzymes make reactions happen that would never occur without them. Which reasoning best evaluates the claim?
options: Wrong: an enzyme speeds a reaction that can already occur and does not change whether it releases energy.
Right: without an enzyme the activation energy of a reaction is infinite, so the reaction has no way to start.
Right: an enzyme provides the energy that an energy-absorbing reaction lacks, so the reaction can go.
Wrong: enzymes change which products form, so they create new reactions instead of speeding old ones.

items.q: Which statement best describes the data at the highest substrate concentration tested?
options: With X the rate is close to the uninhibited rate, while with Y it is about half the uninhibited rate.
Both inhibitors lower the rate to about half of the uninhibited rate at each substrate concentration.
With Y the rate is close to the uninhibited rate, while with X it is about half the uninhibited rate.
Neither inhibitor changes the rate at 32 mM, because the enzyme is saturated with substrate there.

items.q: Which identification of the inhibitors is best supported by the data?
options: X is competitive, since extra substrate brings it toward the uninhibited maximum; Y is noncompetitive, since its maximum stays low.
X is noncompetitive, since it lowers the rate the most at low substrate; Y is competitive, since its rate levels off at a lower value early.
Both are competitive, since both of their curves level off as substrate rises, just as the curve of an uninhibited enzyme does.
Both are noncompetitive, since at 2 mM substrate they give exactly the same rate, 12.5 µmol/min.

items.q: At 8 mM substrate, the rate with inhibitor Y is what percentage of the rate with no inhibitor? Give a whole number.
The experiment is repeated at 100 mM substrate. Which prediction is most consistent with the data?
options: The rate with X will be very close to the uninhibited rate, while the rate with Y will stay near 25 µmol/min.
The rates with X and with Y will both rise to the uninhibited rate, because substrate now far outnumbers each inhibitor.
The rate with Y will rise above the uninhibited rate, because Y slows the reaction less as the substrate builds up.
The rates with X and with Y will both fall, because so much substrate denatures the enzyme in each of the trials.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the shape of the curve with inhibitor Y?
options: Y binds away from the active site and alters the enzyme's shape, so enzymes it binds work poorly at any substrate level.
Y fits the active site so tightly that substrate molecules can push it back out just at very high substrate concentrations.
Y breaks down the substrate before it reaches the enzyme, so less substrate is left to react at each of the concentrations tested.
Y raises the activation energy of the reaction above its uncatalyzed value, so the enzyme makes product more slowly.

items.q: Of the temperatures tested, at which was the reaction fastest when measured at the holding temperature?
Which evidence best shows that the low rate at 25 °C was not caused by damage to the enzyme?
options: After cooling, the 25 °C sample worked at 37 °C as fast (41) as the sample kept at 37 °C (40).
The rate at 25 °C (18) was higher than the rate at 60 °C (6) and at 70 °C (1).
The 25 °C sample was the coldest one tested, and cold slows down chemical reactions in general.
The rate at 25 °C was less than half of the rate at 45 °C, the fastest of the temperatures that were measured.

items.q: The 60 °C sample made product at 6 µmol/min while hot but 14 µmol/min after 30 minutes at 37 °C. Which explanation is most consistent with all the data?
options: Some enzyme molecules unfolded at 60 °C and then refolded on cooling, but most stayed damaged.
The enzyme was not damaged at 60 °C; it just slowed down, as at 25 °C, and then recovered.
Cooling made new enzyme molecules to replace the ones that were destroyed by the heat.
The enzyme works faster at 37 °C than at 60 °C, so the rise in rate shows no change in the enzyme.

items.q: Why did the researchers measure every sample again at 37 °C after cooling?
options: To separate temporary slowing while hot or cold from lasting damage to the enzyme
To give each sample the same total time in the water bath, so that time becomes the independent variable
To find the optimal temperature, which is accurate just when it is measured after cooling
To let the substrate refold after heating, so that it fits the active site again

items.q: After cooling, what percentage of the rate of the sample kept at 37 °C did the 60 °C sample recover? Give a whole number.
At which pH do both enzymes work at more than 10% of their maximum rate?
options: pH 3
pH 4
pH 5
pH 6

items.q: Food moves from the stomach (about pH 2) into the small intestine, where the pH is about 8. What happens to pepsin's activity there, and why?
options: It stops, because at pH 8 pepsin's side chains change charge and its active site no longer works.
It doubles, because a solution at pH 8 has more hydrogen ions available to help the reaction along.
It stays the same, because pepsin's active site is already bound to the substrate it carried from the stomach.
It rises to match trypsin, because both are digestive enzymes that break down proteins.

items.q: Which reasoning best explains why trypsin's rate falls on both sides of pH 8?
options: Moving the pH either way adds or removes hydrogen ions on side chains whose charges the active site needs.
Lower pH speeds the reaction past its maximum and higher pH slows it, so both directions lower the rate.
At pH values away from 8, the substrate dissolves less well in water, so less of it reaches the enzyme.
Trypsin is denatured at each pH other than 8, so its rate is zero at the other pH values tested.

items.q: How many times greater is the hydrogen ion concentration at pepsin's optimal pH than at trypsin's optimal pH? Give the whole number.
Carbonic anhydrase needs a zinc ion held in its active site to work. The zinc ion is best described as
options: a cofactor
a substrate
a competitive inhibitor
a product

items.q: An enzyme needs magnesium ions (Mg²⁺) as a cofactor. EDTA, a chemical that grabs metal ions out of solution, is added, and the rate drops to near zero. Then excess Mg²⁺ is added. What is the most likely result?
options: The rate recovers, because the extra Mg²⁺ is more than the EDTA can hold.
The rate stays near zero, because EDTA unfolded the enzyme when it removed the magnesium.
The rate stays near zero, because magnesium is a substrate that EDTA has already used up.
The rate rises far above its starting value, because the enzyme now has extra cofactor to use.

items.q: An enzyme reaction is running with a very large excess of substrate, and the rate has leveled off. Which change would most increase the rate?
options: Adding more enzyme
Adding more substrate
Adding a competitive inhibitor
Lowering the temperature by 10 °C

items.q: An inhibitor is mixed with an enzyme. The mixture is then placed in a bag with tiny pores that let small molecules such as the inhibitor pass out into a large volume of buffer, but keep the enzyme inside. Which result would show the inhibitor is irreversible?
options: The enzyme still works poorly after the free inhibitor has diffused out of the bag.
The enzyme works normally again after the free inhibitor has diffused out of the bag.
The enzyme works poorly at low substrate but normally at high substrate.
The inhibitor diffuses out of the bag faster than the substrate does.

items.q: A student tests how pH affects the rate of an enzyme. Which set of conditions should be held constant across the trials?
options: Temperature, enzyme amount and substrate amount
pH, temperature and amount of substrate
pH, amount of enzyme and reaction rate
Reaction rate, temperature and the amount of enzyme used

items.q: A human enzyme reaction runs at 37 °C and pH 7 with substrate in large excess, so the rate is at its maximum. Predict the change in the rate after each separate change.

variables.name: Doubling the substrate concentration
Doubling the enzyme concentration
Adding a noncompetitive inhibitor
Cooling the reaction to 27 °C

items.q: A molecule binds an enzyme at a location away from the active site and makes the reaction faster. Which explanation is most likely?
options: It shifts the enzyme into a shape whose active site binds substrate better: allosteric activation.
It acts as a second substrate, so the enzyme makes twice as much product from each reaction.
It competes with the substrate for the active site, pushing out molecules that slow the enzyme down.
It adds energy to the active site, so that substrate molecules can reach the transition state more easily.

items.q: Select the two changes that would lower the maximum rate a sample of enzyme can reach, even with unlimited substrate.
options: Adding a noncompetitive inhibitor
Heating the sample so that part of the enzyme is permanently denatured
Adding a competitive inhibitor
Lowering the substrate concentration
Adding more of the same enzyme

items.q: Methanol is not toxic itself, but an enzyme in the liver converts it to a toxic product. Doctors treat methanol poisoning with fomepizole, a drug that binds the same enzyme's active site and is not converted to a toxic product. Which explanation best fits?
options: Fomepizole competes with methanol for the active site, so less methanol is converted while the body removes it.
Fomepizole binds an allosteric site and changes the enzyme's shape, so that the enzyme is no longer able to bind methanol.
Fomepizole denatures the enzyme permanently, so the liver stops converting methanol until new enzyme is made.
Fomepizole reacts with the toxic product directly and turns it back into methanol, which is harmless.

items.q: Product made by an enzyme was measured at two temperatures: at 37 °C, 10, 20, 48 and 90 µmol after 1, 2, 5 and 10 minutes; at 55 °C, 18, 30, 40 and 41 µmol at the same times. Which interpretation best fits the data?
options: At 55 °C the enzyme starts faster but denatures within minutes, so it makes less product over 10 minutes.
At 55 °C the enzyme runs out of substrate first, because it starts faster and uses the substrate up sooner.
At 37 °C the enzyme is slowly denaturing, which is why its product keeps rising over the 10 minutes.
At 55 °C the enzyme stays active the whole time, but the product breaks down as fast as it forms after 5 minutes.

items.q: Which reactions in the table are exergonic?
options: 1, 4 and 5
2 and 3
1 and 4
2, 3 and 5

items.q: Cells make glutamine by coupling reaction 2 to reaction 1. What is the ΔG of the coupled process, in kJ/mol? Include the sign and give one decimal place.
Making ATP from ADP and Pi is the reverse of reaction 1, so its ΔG is +30.5 kJ/mol. Which claim is supported by the table?
options: Breaking down creatine phosphate can drive ATP synthesis, but breaking down glucose 6-phosphate cannot.
Breaking down glucose 6-phosphate can drive ATP synthesis, because its ΔG is negative.
Neither creatine phosphate nor glucose 6-phosphate can drive ATP synthesis, because ATP synthesis is endergonic.
Both can drive ATP synthesis, because any exergonic reaction can be coupled to any endergonic one.

items.q: In the cell, coupling reaction 1 with reaction 2 happens in two steps on one enzyme. Which description of how the energy is passed on is most accurate?
options: ATP's last phosphate moves onto glutamate, making a less stable intermediate that reacts with NH₃.
ATP is hydrolyzed first, and the heat released warms the glutamate and NH₃ so they react faster.
ATP binds the enzyme's allosteric site, lowering the ΔG of reaction 2 to below zero on its own.
ATP gives its energy to the enzyme, which stores the energy in its structure and later passes it on to glutamate.

items.q: A student claims that a cell can drive a reaction with ΔG = +45.0 kJ/mol by coupling it to the hydrolysis of one ATP. Which response is best?
options: It fails: the total would be +14.5 kJ/mol, so the cell needs two ATP or a larger exergonic partner.
The claim holds: any reaction coupled to ATP hydrolysis goes, because ATP is the cell's energy carrier.
The claim holds: an enzyme lowers the activation energy enough to make the +45.0 reaction go with one ATP.
It fails: endergonic reactions do not occur in cells, whatever exergonic reaction they are coupled to.

items.q: Which statement best describes the data for the normal enzyme 1?
options: Its rate falls steeply as isoleucine rises; the same amounts of valine barely change it.
Its rate falls by about the same amount whether isoleucine or valine is added.
Its rate rises as isoleucine rises and falls as valine rises.
Its rate falls just at 5.0 mM isoleucine, and at lower amounts isoleucine has no clear effect on it.

items.q: Which explanation of the isoleucine results is most consistent with all three columns?
options: Isoleucine binds enzyme 1's allosteric site and changes its shape; the changed site does not bind it.
Isoleucine competes with threonine for enzyme 1's active site, since both are amino acids of a similar size and shape.
Isoleucine denatures enzyme 1, since the rate drops close to zero at the highest amount added.
Isoleucine is broken down by enzyme 1 instead of threonine, so less threonine is converted.

items.q: The strain with the changed enzyme 1 is grown on a medium that already contains plenty of isoleucine. Compared with the normal strain, what is most likely?
options: It keeps making isoleucine it does not need, spending threonine and ATP the normal strain saves.
It stops making isoleucine sooner, because its enzyme 1 is more sensitive to isoleucine.
It makes the same amount of isoleucine, because the medium supplies the isoleucine it needs.
It makes no isoleucine, because a change at the allosteric site also destroys the shape of the active site.

items.q: Why is it an advantage that isoleucine inhibits the first enzyme of the pathway rather than the last?
options: Stopping step 1 keeps threonine and energy from being spent on intermediates that are not needed.
The first enzyme is the one enzyme of the pathway that has an active site, so it is the one that can be inhibited.
The last enzyme makes isoleucine, so inhibiting it would raise the amount of isoleucine in the cell.
Inhibiting the first enzyme lowers the ΔG of each later step, so the pathway runs faster.

items.q: By what percentage does 1.0 mM isoleucine lower the rate of the normal enzyme 1? Give a whole number.
What percentage of the glucose's chemical energy ended up in the new yeast cells? Give a whole number.
Which principle do the data most directly support?
options: The first law: the heat released plus the energy in new cells (109 + 47 kJ) equals the energy in the glucose.
The second law: the heat released (109 kJ) is more than the energy in the new cells (47 kJ).
Energy coupling: the 47 kJ in the new cells came from ATP that the yeast made using the 109 kJ of heat.
Feedback inhibition: the yeast stopped using glucose once its new cells held 47 kJ.

items.q: Why can't the yeast use the 109 kJ of heat to build more cells?
options: Heat is energy spread out as random molecular motion, which cells are unable to capture for work.
The heat was destroyed when it left the yeast cells and entered the calorimeter.
Heat is a form of matter rather than a form of energy, so it does not count toward building new cells.
The heat had already been used once to make ATP, and energy can be used just once.

items.q: The container is opened, the glucose is removed, and the yeast are kept sealed for several days with no food. What is most likely to happen?
options: Without an energy input, the yeast lose their order over time, and their cells break down and die.
The yeast keep their order without food, because their cells already contain the molecules they need for life.
The yeast make new energy from the heat stored in the container, so they keep growing.
The yeast stop releasing any heat, because no energy conversions happen in a cell without food.

items.q: Which statement is the second law of thermodynamics as it applies to cells?
options: Each energy conversion turns some energy into heat, increasing the disorder of the universe.
Energy can be changed from one form to another, but it is not created or destroyed in the process.
Reactions that release energy run faster than reactions that need energy.
Living things create order, so the disorder of the universe decreases over time.

items.q: Joining amino acids into a protein is
options: anabolic and endergonic, so it is coupled to ATP hydrolysis
catabolic and exergonic, so it releases energy the cell can use
anabolic and exergonic, so it goes without any energy input
catabolic and endergonic, so it is coupled to ATP synthesis

items.q: In the overall reaction C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂ → 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O, which statement about electrons is correct?
options: Glucose is oxidized as it loses electrons; oxygen is reduced as it gains them, releasing energy.
Glucose is reduced as it gains electrons from oxygen, which stores energy in the carbon dioxide made.
Oxygen is oxidized as it loses electrons to glucose, and the water formed holds most of the energy.
No electrons move, because each atom on the left side of the equation also appears in the products on the right.

items.q: A resting adult holds about 50 g of ATP in the body but hydrolyzes about 50 kg of ATP per day. Which claim do these numbers best support?
options: Each ATP molecule is remade from ADP and Pi about a thousand times a day, so ATP carries energy rather than storing it.
The body stores most of its energy in the form of ATP, which is why it holds as much as 50 g at any moment.
The body makes 50 kg of new adenine, ribose and phosphate each day to build fresh ATP.
ATP hydrolysis releases so much energy that a person needs just 50 g of food per day to supply it.

items.q: Select the two examples of energy coupling.
options: A membrane pump uses ATP hydrolysis to move sodium ions against their concentration gradient.
A muscle protein uses ATP hydrolysis to change shape and pull on a fiber.
Sweat evaporating from skin carries heat away from the body.
Glucose diffusing into a cell through a channel protein down its gradient.
A hot plate warming a beaker of water.

items.q: A poison stops a cell from making ATP. Predict the change in each variable over the next few minutes.

variables.name: ATP concentration in the cell
ADP concentration in the cell
Concentration difference of sodium ions across the membrane
Number of sodium-potassium pump proteins in the membrane

items.q: In the ATP cycle, which process supplies the energy to turn ADP and Pi back into ATP?
options: Exergonic reactions that break down food molecules
Endergonic reactions that build proteins from amino acids
Heat released by other reactions in the cell
Hydrolysis of other ATP molecules in the same cell

items.q: In which range of wavelengths is the rate of O₂ release lowest?
options: 525-575 nm (green)
425-475 nm (blue)
400-425 nm (violet)

items.q: At 475 nm, chlorophyll a absorbs only 12% as strongly as at its peak, yet O₂ release is 85% of maximum. Which explanation do the data best support?
options: Chlorophyll b and carotenoids absorb strongly at 475 nm and pass the energy on to chlorophyll a in the photosystems.
Light at 475 nm carries more energy per photon, so the little that chlorophyll a absorbs is enough to drive photosynthesis at full speed.
Carotenoids split water themselves at 475 nm, producing O₂ without any help from chlorophyll a or the photosystems.
The action spectrum was measured on living cells, so its values are higher than absorption at each wavelength.

items.q: Two identical cultures of these algae are grown for a week, one under light of 550 nm and one under light of 450 nm at the same intensity. What is the most likely result?
options: The culture under 550 nm grows less, because its pigments absorb little of that light.
The culture under 550 nm grows more, because green light is the color algae reflect and use best.
Both grow the same, because the two lights have the same intensity and so deliver the same usable energy.
The culture under 450 nm grows less, because carotenoids absorb blue light and block it from chlorophyll.

items.q: A long strand of alga is lit with a spectrum spread from violet to red along its length. Bacteria that swim toward higher O₂ are added. Where will the bacteria gather most?
options: Along the blue and red parts of the strand
Along the green and yellow parts of the strand
Evenly along the whole strand
Along the violet end, where the light energy per photon is highest

items.q: In tube A, what is the average rate of change in absorbance over the 20 minutes, in absorbance units per minute? Give the size of the change (no sign) to three decimal places.
What does the fall in absorbance in tube A show?
options: Illuminated chloroplasts released electrons, which reduced the DCPIP and turned it colorless.
Illuminated chloroplasts made sugar, which mixed with the DCPIP and diluted its blue color.
Light alone bleached the DCPIP, because light energy breaks down blue dyes over time.
Chloroplasts in the light took in DCPIP through their membranes, removing it from the solution.

items.q: Which comparison shows that the reaction in tube A requires working chloroplast proteins, not just chloroplast material?
options: Tube A with tube C
Tube A with tube B
Tube A with tube D
Tube B with tube D

items.q: In tube E, DCMU blocks electrons from leaving photosystem II. Which prediction about tube E is best supported?
options: O₂ release and H⁺ pumping by the cytochrome complex both stop, because electron flow through the chain stops.
O₂ release continues, because water splitting happens before the block, but no NADPH or ATP is made.
ATP is still made at the normal rate, because ATP synthase does not depend on electron transport.
Photosystem I keeps reducing DCPIP at the normal rate, because it receives its electrons directly from water.

items.q: In an intact chloroplast, which molecule receives the electrons that DCPIP receives in this experiment?
options: NADP⁺
O₂
CO₂
ATP

items.q: Which statement best describes the data?
options: Below 20% light the two curves overlap, but above 40% the leaf at 0.10% CO₂ takes up clearly more CO₂.
At each light intensity, the leaf at 0.10% CO₂ takes up about twice as much CO₂ as the leaf at 0.04%.
At 0.04% CO₂ uptake keeps rising steadily up to full sunlight, while at 0.10% it levels off early.
In the dark both leaves take up a small amount of CO₂, about 1.5 µmol/m²/s.

items.q: Which factor most limits photosynthesis at 10% light and at 80% light in normal air (0.04% CO₂)?
options: At 10%, light intensity; at 80%, CO₂ concentration
At 10%, CO₂ concentration; at 80%, light intensity
At both, light intensity
At both, CO₂ concentration

items.q: Why is net CO₂ uptake negative at 0% light?
options: With no light, photosynthesis stops but the leaf's cells keep releasing CO₂ by cellular respiration.
With no light, the Calvin cycle runs backward and breaks sugar down, releasing CO₂ from the stroma.
With no light, the stomata release the CO₂ stored in the leaf during the earlier light treatments.
Negative values are measurement errors, because a leaf is unable to release more CO₂ than it takes in.

items.q: At full sunlight (100%), by what percentage does raising CO₂ from 0.04% to 0.10% increase net CO₂ uptake? Give a whole number.
The run at 0.10% CO₂ and full sunlight is repeated with the chamber cooled from 25 °C to 10 °C. Which prediction is best supported?
options: Net CO₂ uptake will fall, because the Calvin cycle's enzymes run more slowly in the cold.
Net CO₂ uptake will rise, because the cold leaf respires less and so releases less CO₂.
Net CO₂ uptake will stay at 18.3, because light and CO₂ are the main factors that control photosynthesis, and neither changed.
Net CO₂ uptake will fall to zero, because chlorophyll stops absorbing light at 10 °C.

items.q: Which claim do the results for samples 1-3 best support?
options: A difference in H⁺ concentration across the thylakoid membrane is enough to make ATP, even with no light.
Light is needed for ATP synthase to make ATP, because no sample made ATP in the dark.
Thylakoids make ATP whenever they are placed in a buffer of pH 8, whatever treatment they had beforehand.
Thylakoids make ATP when their inside is less acidic than the buffer around them.

items.q: Why did sample 4, with a chemical that lets H⁺ leak across membranes, make almost no ATP?
options: H⁺ leaked across the membrane instead of through ATP synthase, so the gradient ran down without making ATP.
The chemical destroyed the ADP and Pi in the second buffer, so ATP synthase had nothing to join together into ATP.
The chemical blocked the channel of ATP synthase, as the drug in sample 5 did.
The chemical raised the pH inside the thylakoids to 4, so the inside became more acidic.

items.q: A new sample is soaked at pH 4 and moved to pH 9 instead of pH 8. Compared with sample 1, how much ATP is it most likely to make?
options: More, because the H⁺ gradient is ten times steeper and stores more energy.
Less, because a pH of 9 is too basic for ATP synthase to work properly.
The same, because ATP synthase makes ATP at one fixed rate when any gradient is present.
Very little, because H⁺ flow through ATP synthase works just at pH 8 outside.

items.q: Why did the researchers keep the thylakoids in the dark for the whole experiment?
options: So light could not build an H⁺ gradient by electron transport, leaving the pH difference as the energy source.
So the pigments would not absorb the ATP produced by ATP synthase and break it down again into ADP and Pi.
So the thylakoids would not split the buffer's water and change its pH from 8 to some other value.
So the Calvin cycle would run, since it works best in the dark and would use up any ATP that was made in the light.

items.q: Where does the Calvin cycle take place, and which products of the light reactions does it use?
options: In the stroma, using ATP and NADPH
In the thylakoid space, using ATP and O₂
In the thylakoid membrane, using light and water
In the stroma, using O₂ and glucose

items.q: Algae were given water containing heavy oxygen (¹⁸O) and normal CO₂. A second batch got normal water and CO₂ containing ¹⁸O. In which batch will the O₂ released contain ¹⁸O, and why?
options: The first batch, because O₂ comes from splitting water at photosystem II.
The second batch, because the O₂ is released when carbon is removed from CO₂ in the Calvin cycle.
Both batches equally, because O₂ is made from a mixture of the oxygen in water and in CO₂.
Neither batch, because ¹⁸O is too heavy to be built into molecules by living cells.

items.q: Which observation best supports the idea that chloroplasts descend from cyanobacteria?
options: Chloroplasts have their own circular DNA and photosystems very similar to those of cyanobacteria.
Chloroplasts are found in plant cells but not in animal cells, which use mitochondria instead.
Chloroplasts are green, and green is the most common color of bacteria found in ponds and lakes.
Chloroplasts make sugar, and bacteria in general are able to make sugar from carbon dioxide and water.

items.q: Select the two products of the light reactions that the Calvin cycle uses directly.
options: ATP
NADPH
O₂
CO₂
Glucose

items.q: The Calvin cycle is sometimes called the light-independent reactions. A student claims it therefore runs fastest at night. Which response is best?
options: The claim is wrong: the cycle needs ATP and NADPH from the light reactions, so it slows within minutes of darkness.
The claim is right: without light the light reactions stop, leaving more chloroplast resources for the Calvin cycle.
The claim is right: the Calvin cycle's enzymes are damaged by light, so they work best at night when it is dark.
The claim is wrong: the Calvin cycle needs light to be absorbed directly by its enzymes in the stroma at each step.

items.q: A plant that has been in bright light is suddenly moved into darkness. Predict the change in each variable over the next few minutes.

variables.name: O₂ released by the chloroplasts
H⁺ concentration in the thylakoid space
Rate of CO₂ fixation by the Calvin cycle
Amount of chlorophyll in the leaf

items.q: In the thylakoid membrane, what does the energy released by electrons moving along the electron transport chain do?
options: It pumps H⁺ from the stroma into the thylakoid space, building a gradient that drives ATP synthase.
It joins ADP and Pi directly, with each electron that passes making one ATP at the cytochrome complex.
It splits CO₂ into carbon and O₂, which is the source of the oxygen released by plants in the light.
It is stored as heat in the thylakoid space, which warms the Calvin cycle's enzymes so they work faster.

items.q: Correct the germinating peas at 25 °C using the beads-only vial at 25 °C. What is their average rate of O₂ use over the 20 minutes, in mL per minute? Give three decimal places.
Why does each vial contain KOH?
options: It removes the CO₂ the peas release, so the change in gas volume shows O₂ taken up alone.
It supplies O₂ to the peas, so that they can keep respiring for the full 20 minutes.
It keeps the temperature inside each vial steady, so that the water bath does not warm the gas.
It kills bacteria on the peas, so that just the peas' own respiration is measured in the vial.

items.q: What is the purpose of the vials containing beads only?
options: They show volume changes not caused by respiration, such as shifts in temperature or pressure.
They show how much O₂ the glass beads themselves use, so that the beads can be subtracted from the dry-pea vial.
They give the peas in the other vials extra space, so that the peas do not run out of O₂.
They show the O₂ use of germinating peas at a lower rate, for comparison with the dry peas.

items.q: Why do germinating peas use O₂ much faster than dry peas at the same temperature?
options: Germinating peas break down stored starch for ATP to grow; dry peas are dormant, with little metabolism.
Dry peas carry out photosynthesis inside the vial, which releases O₂ and hides their uptake of O₂.
Germinating peas are larger than dry peas, so more of their surface absorbs KOH and makes the drop move.
Dry peas lack mitochondria until they absorb water, so they are unable to carry out cellular respiration in the vial.

items.q: Corrected O₂ use by germinating peas is 0.82 mL at 25 °C and 0.32 mL at 10 °C over 20 minutes. Which explanation and prediction are best supported?
options: Respiration's enzymes run slower at 10 °C, so at 30 °C the peas would likely use O₂ faster than at 25 °C.
Cold denatures the enzymes of respiration, so the peas at 10 °C would not recover if they were warmed again.
Peas at 10 °C need less ATP because they are colder, so they switch from respiration to photosynthesis.
The KOH absorbs CO₂ more slowly at 10 °C, so the cold vials show less gas taken up than was really used.

items.q: During which interval did the mitochondria use O₂ fastest?
options: 2-6 min
6-10 min

items.q: What was the rate of O₂ use between 2 and 6 minutes, in nmol/mL per minute? Give a whole number.
After oligomycin blocks ATP synthase at 6 minutes, O₂ use falls sharply even though the electron transport chain itself is not blocked. Why?
options: H⁺ is no longer able to flow back through ATP synthase, so the gradient grows until the chain stalls.
Oligomycin also blocks the last protein of the chain, so O₂ is unable to accept electrons from it.
Without ATP synthase working, the matrix runs out of the O₂ that ATP synthase normally releases.
The ADP added at 2 minutes has been used up by then, and ADP is the molecule that the chain hands its electrons to.

items.q: DNP, added at 10 minutes, carries H⁺ across membranes. Which statement about the period from 10 to 14 minutes is best supported?
options: O₂ use is fast because H⁺ leaks back through DNP, so the chain runs freely, but the energy becomes heat, not ATP.
O₂ use is fast because DNP unblocks ATP synthase, so the mitochondria are now making more ATP than at any earlier time.
O₂ use is fast because DNP is itself broken down using O₂, and the mitochondria use it as a fuel.
O₂ use is fast because DNP is an electron carrier that delivers extra electrons from pyruvate to the chain.

items.q: Why did O₂ use stop completely after cyanide was added, even though DNP was still present?
options: Cyanide stops electrons from reaching O₂, so no O₂ is reduced to water.
Cyanide blocks the H⁺ leak through DNP, so the gradient rebuilds and stops the pumping.
Cyanide uses up the O₂ left in the chamber by reacting with it directly.
Cyanide blocks ATP synthase, which had started making ATP again once DNP was added.

items.q: In the flask without O₂, how many molecules of CO₂ were released per molecule of glucose used? Give one decimal place.
Assume about 30 ATP per glucose with O₂ and 2 per glucose without. Which claim do the data support?
options: With O₂ the yeast made about 3.5 times more ATP while using under a quarter as much glucose.
Without O₂ the yeast made more ATP, because they used over four times as much glucose.
The two flasks made about the same amount of ATP, because both released a similar amount of CO₂.
Without O₂ the yeast made no ATP, because ethanol and CO₂ were the sole products they made.

items.q: Why do yeast without O₂ turn pyruvate into ethanol instead of simply stopping after glycolysis?
options: Making ethanol passes NADH's electrons on, regenerating NAD⁺ so glycolysis can keep running.
Making ethanol releases more ATP than glycolysis, which is the main energy source without O₂.
Ethanol is the final electron acceptor of the electron transport chain when no O₂ is available.
Ethanol is needed to build new yeast cells, so the yeast make it in large amounts whether O₂ is present or not.

items.q: In the flask with O₂, the yeast released 2.70 mmol CO₂ from 0.45 mmol glucose. What does this ratio show?
options: About 6 CO₂ per glucose: all six carbons were oxidized, as in aerobic respiration.
About 2 CO₂ per glucose, so the yeast fermented glucose to ethanol even when O₂ was present.
About 0.17 CO₂ per glucose, so most of the glucose's carbon was kept as ethanol.
About 6 CO₂ per glucose, which shows the CO₂ came from the O₂ that was bubbled into the flask.

items.q: Which claim is best supported by the data?
options: UCP1 is needed for brown fat to produce enough heat to keep a mouse warm in the cold.
UCP1 is needed for brown-fat mitochondria to make ATP, which the mice burn to stay warm.
Mice lacking UCP1 have no brown fat, so their mitochondria use less O₂ in each tissue of the body.
Mice lacking UCP1 keep their body temperature as well as normal mice by shivering instead.

items.q: Normal brown-fat mitochondria used O₂ rapidly even with no ADP added. Which explanation fits?
options: H⁺ leaks back into the matrix through UCP1, so the gradient stays low and the chain keeps going.
UCP1 makes ATP from AMP instead of ADP, so the mitochondria do not need any ADP added to run.
UCP1 carries electrons straight to O₂, so the electron transport chain in brown fat is bypassed.
Brown-fat mitochondria store large amounts of ADP, so adding more ADP had no effect on their use of O₂.

items.q: Compared with muscle mitochondria, how much ATP would you expect normal brown-fat mitochondria to make for each O₂ molecule they use?
options: Less, because many H⁺ return through UCP1 instead of ATP synthase.
More, because they use O₂ faster, and faster O₂ use means more ATP.
The same, because each mitochondrion makes a fixed amount of ATP per O₂.
More, because their extra heat speeds up ATP synthase.

items.q: Why were the isolated brown-fat mitochondria given fuel but no ADP when their O₂ use was measured?
options: With ATP synthase idle, any O₂ use reflects H⁺ returning by another route, such as UCP1.
ADP would have reacted with the fuel and used it up before the mitochondria could take any in.
Without ADP the mitochondria make extra ATP, which makes the difference between the two groups larger.
ADP is toxic to isolated mitochondria from mice that lack UCP1, so it had to be left out of both groups.

items.q: Where in a eukaryotic cell does the Krebs cycle take place?
options: In the mitochondrial matrix
In the cytosol
In the inner mitochondrial membrane
In the intermembrane space

items.q: A rat is fed glucose in which every carbon atom is radioactive, and it breathes normal air. Where will most of the radioactive carbon appear first outside the body?
options: In the CO₂ the rat breathes out
In the water the rat breathes out
In the O₂ the rat breathes out
In the urea in the rat's urine

items.q: In a human muscle cell, select the two stages that release CO₂.
options: Pyruvate oxidation
Krebs cycle
Glycolysis
Electron transport chain
Lactic acid fermentation

items.q: Select the statement that is true of fermentation in human muscle cells.
options: It regenerates NAD⁺ by passing electrons from NADH to pyruvate.
It makes about 30 ATP per glucose when O₂ runs low.
It uses the electron transport chain with lactate as the final electron acceptor.
It takes place in the mitochondrial matrix.
It releases CO₂ from each pyruvate.

items.q: Cyanide is added to cultured human cells, blocking the last protein of the electron transport chain. Predict the change in each variable over the next few minutes.

variables.name: O₂ used by the cells
H⁺ concentration in the intermembrane space
ATP made by oxidative phosphorylation
Lactate made by the cells
Number of mitochondria in each cell

items.q: A gram of fat yields more than twice as much ATP as a gram of glucose when oxidized. Which explanation is best?
options: Fatty acids have far more hydrogen and less oxygen per carbon, so they supply more electrons to the chain.
Fats are broken down by glycolysis twice, because each fat molecule contains two glucose units joined by an ester bond.
Fats are oxidized in the cytosol, where ATP synthase works faster than it does inside the mitochondria.
Fats skip the electron transport chain and make their ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation instead.

items.q: Which comparison of chemiosmosis in chloroplasts and in mitochondria is correct?
options: Chloroplasts pump H⁺ into the thylakoid space and make ATP in the stroma; mitochondria pump into the intermembrane space and make ATP in the matrix.
In both, H⁺ is pumped into the same compartment where ATP is made, and then flows back out through ATP synthase.
In chloroplasts the electrons come from glucose; in mitochondria they come from splitting water.
In chloroplasts O₂ is the final electron acceptor; in mitochondria NADP⁺ is the final electron acceptor.

items.q: In a cell that cannot ferment, removing O₂ soon stops glycolysis too, although glycolysis itself uses no O₂. Why?
options: With the chain stopped, NADH has nowhere to unload and NAD⁺ runs out, so glycolysis stalls.
Glycolysis needs the ATP made by the chain as its starting energy, and the chain makes no ATP when O₂ is missing.
Without O₂ the cytosol becomes too acidic for the enzymes of glycolysis, which denature within seconds.
Pyruvate turns into O₂ when O₂ is absent, and this O₂ blocks the first enzyme of glycolysis by feedback.
